title: Reduced-subword criterion via increasing root-reflection chains
statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space [def-weil-vector-space-dimension] with a positive definite symmetric bilinear form $(\ ,\ )$. Let $\Phi\subseteq V\setminus\{0\}$ be finite and span $V$, and suppose that $\Phi\cap\mathbf R\alpha=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$ for each $\alpha\in\Phi$, that $s_\alpha(v)=v-2(v,\alpha)(\alpha,\alpha)^{-1}\alpha$ permutes $\Phi$, and that $2(\beta,\alpha)/(\alpha,\alpha)\in\mathbf Z$ for all roots $\alpha,\beta$. Let $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ be a real vector-space basis such that each root has integer $\Delta$-coordinates all nonnegative or all nonpositive. Put $\Phi^+=\{\beta\in\Phi:\text{all its }\Delta\text{-coordinates are nonnegative}\}$. Let $W_\Delta$ be the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbf R}(V)$ generated by $\{s_\alpha:\alpha\in\Delta\}$. For $w\in W_\Delta$, let $\ell(w)$ be the least number of simple reflections in an expression for $w$, and call such a minimal expression reduced. For $u,v\in W_\Delta$, the following conditions are equivalent: (i) some reduced expression for $v$ contains, in its original order, a subsequence of letters that is a reduced expression for $u$; (ii) there are an integer $m\geq0$, elements $x_0,\ldots,x_m\in W_\Delta$ and roots $\gamma_0,\ldots,\gamma_{m-1}\in\Phi$ such that $$x_0=u,\qquad x_m=v,\qquad x_{i+1}=x_i s_{\gamma_i},\qquad\ell(x_i)<\ell(x_{i+1})\quad(0\leq i<m).$$ The case $m=0$ is permitted and means $u=v$. The equivalence also holds for the empty root system, where $W_\Delta=\{1\}$.

source.place: Definition 2.1.1, printed p.27, Lemma 2.2.1 and Theorem 2.2.2 with Corollary 2.2.3, printed pp.33--34; root-reflection identification in Proposition 4.4.5, printed p.104. Applicability to the present real-root formulation: Milne iAG2017 Appendix C.11 and C.22, printed pp.610,612. Local Björner--Brenti PDF WANTED; university-hosted text read online.

proof.text: Put $P=\Phi^+$ and $D=\Delta$. Direct substitution in the reflection formula gives $s_a^2=1$, $s_a(a)=-a$ and $(s_ax,s_ay)=(x,y)$: on expanding, the two cross terms $-4(x,a)(y,a)/(a,a)$ cancel the quadratic term $4(x,a)(y,a)/(a,a)$. Thus every simple-reflection word and its inverse preserve the form and permute $\Phi$. Since no root is zero and the base coordinates have one sign, $\Phi=P\sqcup(-P)$ and $D\subseteq P$. If $\Phi=\varnothing$, spanning gives $V=0$ and $W_\Delta=\{1\}$; the empty reduced word and $m=0$ give both conditions. Henceforth assume $\Phi\ne\varnothing$.

source.place: Appendix C.8 and C.21, printed pp.609,612; explicit calculation and empty-root case.

proof.text: For $a\in D$ and $b\in P\setminus\{a\}$, reducedness of $\Phi$ implies that some coordinate of $b$ at a simple root other than $a$ is positive. The reflection $s_a$ changes only the $a$-coordinate. The root $s_ab$ therefore still has that positive coordinate, so all its coordinates are nonnegative. Moreover $s_ab\ne a$, since otherwise $b=s_aa=-a$. Hence $s_a(P\setminus\{a\})\subseteq P\setminus\{a\}$; involutivity gives equality. These are precisely the sign-partition and simple-sign-preservation hypotheses of the word-deletion statement used below.

source.place: Appendix C.9--C.11 and C.21, printed pp.609--610,612; elementary coordinate verification of the sign-deletion hypotheses.

proof.text:
Apply simple-root-reflection generation with $R=\Phi$ and $D=\Delta$: every $s_b$, $b\in\Phi$, belongs to $W_\Delta$. All its hypotheses are those of the item. For any $h\in W_\Delta$, form preservation gives, by evaluating on $z\in V$,
$$h^{-1}s_a h(z)=z-2(hz,a)(a,a)^{-1}h^{-1}a=s_{h^{-1}a}(z).$$
Here $h^{-1}a\in\Phi$. Thus every conjugate of a simple reflection is a root reflection. Also $s_{-b}=s_b$ directly from the formula. We will normalize any root defining a reflection to its positive choice in $P$.

source.place: Appendix C.11 first assertion and C.8, printed pp.609--610; direct conjugation calculation.

proof.text:
Fix $b\in P$. If $wb\in-P$, apply sign-word deletion to a reduced simple word for $w$: it gives a word for $ws_b$ with one fewer letter, hence $\ell(ws_b)<\ell(w)$. If $wb\in P$, set $y=ws_b\in W_\Delta$. Then $yb=-wb\in-P$, so the preceding argument gives $\ell(w)=\ell(ys_b)<\ell(y)$. Consequently
$$\ell(ws_b)<\ell(w)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ wb\in-P,$$
and the two lengths are never equal. In the decreasing case, applying sign-word deletion to ANY simple word for $w$ removes exactly one letter and gives $ws_b$, whether or not that word is reduced. By step 3, every $t\in T=\{h^{-1}s_a h:h\in W_\Delta,\ a\in\Delta\}$ is a root reflection. Thus $\ell(wt)\leq\ell(w)$ implies one-letter deletion from any simple word for $w$: this is right strong exchange with $\leq$. The assumptions on $S$ also hold: every $s_a$ is an involution different from $1$, and the definition of $W_\Delta$ gives finite products because inverses of the generators equal themselves.

source.place: Theorem 1.4.3, printed pp.15--16, and the exchange hypothesis used in Lemma 2.2.1; real-root verification supplied here from the cited sign-word-deletion statement.

proof.text: Every simple word contains a reduced subword with the same product. Here are the deletion details. Multiplying by one simple reflection changes length by at most one, since a word for either factor-product can be extended to a word for the other. Step 4 excludes equality, so the change is exactly one. In a nonreduced word choose its first nonreduced prefix, of length $j$, and let $p$ be the preceding prefix-product; thus $\ell(p)=j-1$ and $\ell(ps_a)=j-2$. Step 4 gives $pa\in-P$. Sign-word deletion on the $(j-1)$ letters representing $p$ expresses $ps_a$ by omitting one of those letters. Restoring the untouched suffix deletes two positions from the original word without changing its product. Induction on the original word length now gives a reduced subword: the reduced case is the base, and otherwise this shorter word is still a subsequence of the original word. This is a finite deletion argument, not an assumption that every subword of a reduced word is reduced.

source.place: Proposition 1.4.7 and Corollary 1.4.8(i), printed pp.17--18; the short induction is written out from sign-word deletion.

proof.text: Assume (ii), and fix any reduced word for $v=x_m$. Work backwards through the chain. At an edge $x_{i+1}=x_i s_{\gamma_i}$, normalize $\gamma_i$ to $b\in P$; then $x_i=x_{i+1}s_b$ and its length is smaller. Step 4 gives $x_{i+1}b\in-P$. Sign-word deletion therefore deletes a single letter from the current word for $x_{i+1}$ and yields a word for $x_i$. Its hypotheses were verified in steps 1--2 and require no reducedness of that current word. Induction down to $i=0$ gives a word for $u$ that is a subsequence of the fixed word for $v$. Apply the finite deletion argument of step 5 to that word; the resulting reduced word for $u$ is still a subsequence of the chosen reduced word for $v$. This proves (i).

source.place: Theorem 2.2.2, printed p.34, chain-to-subword direction; keeps the intermediate words possibly nonreduced.

proof.text:
Assume (i) and fix a witnessing reduced word $s_{a_1}\cdots s_{a_q}$ for $v$. Induct on $d=q-\ell(u)\geq0$, with this fixed word. If $d=0$, its reduced subword for $u$ occupies all $q$ positions, so $u=v$ and $m=0$ works. If $d>0$, then $u\ne v$ and the one-letter-extension node applies: its group, generating-involution and strong-exchange hypotheses were verified in steps 1, 3 and 4. It supplies positions $I$ and an omitted position $r$ such that the selected word for $u$ is reduced and inserting $s_{a_r}$ gives a reduced word with product $z$ and length $\ell(u)+1$. Let $A$ be the product of the selected letters before $r$ and $B$ the product of those after $r$. Then
$$u=AB,\quad z=A s_{a_r}B=u(B^{-1}s_{a_r}B)=u s_{B^{-1}a_r}.$$
The vector $B^{-1}a_r$ is a root and the last identity is the explicit conjugation calculation in step 3. Thus $u\longrightarrow z$ is one permitted edge with strictly increasing length. The reduced word for $z$ is a subword of the same fixed word for $v$, and $q-\ell(z)=d-1$. The induction hypothesis supplies a permitted finite chain from $z$ to $v$; prepend this edge. This proves (ii). The same $m=0$ argument handles $u=v$ independently of rank.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.1 and Theorem 2.2.2, printed pp.33--34; induction on the number of missing letters, with the right root reflection calculated explicitly.
